Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Arthur Vance had been twenty-two when the mortar struck the ridge outside his forward operating base in the Helmand Valley. He was certain that the ground simply gave way, followed by a sky of shattered dust and the sharp, metallic cracks of incoming rounds. He remembered the heat pressing against his face, the sudden silence of the men beside him, and the heavy, wet guilt that settled in his chest as he pulled himself from the dirt. He had come to believe that surviving when others did not was a quiet betrayal. In the months that followed, that initial shock crystallized into a steady, unspoken terror. When he closed his eyes, the valley would rise again with all its original force, and the same terror that had once locked his knees would flood his body. He knew exactly what had happened, yet when his partner asked him to explain it, he would stare at the kitchen table, his mouth opening and closing as he could not find words to describe it. The days bled into years as Arthur built a life around the edges of that memory. He began to view the world as a dangerous place, a landscape where any sudden sound or shifting routine could unspool him. He stopped wearing the faded olive-drab field jacket he had kept from deployment, folding it away in a cedar chest while the fabric and cut still mirrored the uniform he had worn on the ridge. He refused to go near the specific valley where the strike occurred, telling himself it was merely a preference, though he would turn his truck a mile out of his way to pass that stretch of highway. Thinking about the event became something to be managed rather than faced; he would deliberately steer conversations toward the weather or the weathered work schedules on his breakroom bulletin board, keeping the heavy, unspoken past at bay. His identity felt untethered. He had come to believe that the man he was before the ridge no longer fit him, that he moved through his own life like a ghost wearing familiar skin. At his current job in a sprawling warehouse on the city’s industrial edge, these habits took on concrete shape. Arthur worked the receiving bay, where the heavy canvas work boots he now wore daily echoed the tread of his old issue boots, and where the high metal racks and rolling steel doors mirrored the outpost’s layout. When the bay doors clanged shut on a particularly hot afternoon, the sound caught in his throat, and he would stand perfectly still until the echo faded. His relationship had shifted around this quiet withdrawal; his partner had learned not to press him when he grew still during stories, nor to hang up the olive jacket on the back of the hallway chair where he could see it. Over the years, these avoided locations, the hidden jacket, and the careful management of his thoughts had accumulated into a life that felt carefully measured but narrowing. His relief work schedule had shortened, and he no longer volunteered for the overtime runs that took him past the valley exits. What finally brought Arthur to seek help was not a sudden crisis but a gradual suffocation. He sat in the waiting room with a manila folder on his lap, his hands resting on the worn denim of his trousers. He was most afraid that the quiet space around him was actually a trap, that he would one day find himself utterly alone with a memory he could not name. Yet, beneath the hesitation, there was a steady hope that someone might help him sort through the unspoken dust, that he might once again find the words without losing the peace he had fought to keep.
